contentGaps: No ranking page gives a formula: eye height minus camera/head offset plus lean and terrain allowance
Head offset: a tilt head adds inches while a side-mount MonoGimbal drops the camera (one 6'8" BCG owner found the MH-100 too low)
The lean technique (Photography Mad, DPReview) means the monopod must be 'too long' for vertical use
Slopes and shooting up into trees: a 6'6" BCG owner needed a foot more than a 64" monopod
A table by photographer height (CDC average men 68.9 in, women 63.5 in)

outline.intent: Direct answer: max height (with head) at or a little above your eye height, plus 6-12 in if you lean it or shoot on slopes

titlePattern.gap: No title gives a sizing chart or formula by the reader's height; angle: exact keyword first plus 'a height chart' / 'by your height'.

commonPoints: The monopod plus head should bring the viewfinder to eye level
Tall photographers need longer monopods than standard 60-64 in models
The head adds a few inches
Leaning the monopod forward is a stable stance and needs extra length
You should not have to bend over

ourGain.point: A simple formula: eye height minus camera and head offset, plus 6-12 in for lean and slopes
Height chart built on CDC average heights (men 68.9 in, women 63.5 in) rather than vague 'tall person' advice
Head choice changes the number: a side-mount MonoGimbal hangs the camera lower; one 6'8" owner went back to a tilt head
Terrain allowance: a 6'6" owner needed about a foot more than a 64 in monopod on a riverbank and shooting into trees; screw-on extension columns fix a short monopod

painPoints.pain: Picking a monopod height that still reaches the eye on slopes, banks and snow
painPoints.details: Wildlife shooters tilting up with long lenses lose eye-level; the monopod sinks into snow or debris and bending over defeats the purpose.

quotes.text: The monopod needs to be taller to account for the rough terrain and it will settle through snow or debris.
You don't want to bend over with a monopod.

painPoints.pain: Holding a big lens steady for minutes or hours tires the arms
painPoints.details: Wildlife and sports shooters waiting for action cannot keep a heavy tele on target and consider a monopod to take the weight.

quotes.text: when waiting for action, I cannot hold the lens steady for minutes
Better to use a monopod than to fight arm fatigue late in the second half of a game.

painPoints.pain: Long collapsed length makes a hiking pole or monopod awkward in a pack or on a flight
painPoints.details: Poles that collapse to around 27 in stick out of bags and complicate air travel.

quotes.text: Shorter collapsed length will greatly simplify travel with your poles.
it might be too long for carry-on, or easy carry in a pack/bag.

painPoints.pain: Compact travel tripods are too short, forcing photographers to bend over
painPoints.details: Tall users find folded-small tripods stop well below eye level once the center column is left down.

quotes.text: a travel pod will be shorter requiring you to bend over to look through the VF
the CP30 S4 II is too short for general use
